findings.evidence: Wrenford "nomu" = three: misheard: mumu → momu → nomu (generation 18) · Wrenford "deku" = no: misheard: diku → deku (generation 3) · Oakhollow "dole" = ore: misheard: dule → dole (generation 24)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.75, p = 0.006, n = 12. Most used: two (2% replaced per generation), tools (25% replaced per generation), wood (15% replaced per generation); least: four (43%), five (69%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 14, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.68, p = <0.001, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
